title: World Literature
tagline: Greece and Rome, the Bible and the Middle Ages, the Renaissance, classicism and the Enlightenment, Romanticism, the realist novel, Russian literature, modernism, post-war and contemporary literature, Asian, African and Latin American literature, and translation and reception
summary: Modern Chinese literature grew up in conversation with foreign literature, read mostly in translation. This course surveys the literatures of the world from Homer and Greek tragedy through Dante, Shakespeare, the Enlightenment, Romanticism and the great realist and Russian novels to modernism and contemporary writing, together with the literatures of Japan, India, the Arab world, Africa and Latin America, and asks what is gained and lost in translation.
overview: This course is not a shorter history of every literature on earth; nobody can teach that honestly. It is a course about a relation: the relation between a text written in one place and the set of institutions - translation, schooling, prizes, copyright, publishing lists - that later make it available somewhere else. Once the relation is the object, the interesting questions change: not 'is this great' but 'how did it arrive'.

We move through the usual periods in a fast but honest sweep - Greece and Rome, the Bible and the Middle Ages, the Renaissance, the Enlightenment, Romanticism, realism, the Russian nineteenth century, modernism, the postwar period - and then turn to the literatures that the old European syllabus kept at the edge: the Arabic and Persian traditions, Sanskrit and classical Japanese, African writing, and the Latin American boom that taught the twentieth century how to read the twentieth century.

A second thread runs across the whole course: the material history of circulation. Oral poetry and its transcription, the codex and the scroll, paper and woodblock, print, the cheap serial, the paperback, the copyright act, the translation grant, the prize, the algorithmic shelf. Each of these changes what counts as literature before it changes what is written.

The final chapter is the course's test. We read the major recent proposals for 'world literature' as positions in an argument about the periphery and the centre, about translation as loss and as the condition of existence, and about who pays for the distance a text travels.
outcomes: Summarise the major periods, genres and works of several literary traditions well enough to place a text in a genealogy rather than a country.
Analyse a literary work with attention to the conventions it inherits (epic, tragedy, romance, sonnet, novel, chronicle) and to the transaction those conventions make with an audience.
Explain how material conditions - orality, manuscript, print, serialisation, digitisation - shape form, and give period-specific examples.
Use the vocabulary of comparatism (influence, reception, translation, adaptation, borrowing, canon, world-system) without collapsing it into the vocabulary of influence-anxiety.
Read translation as a practice with costs and beneficiaries, and evaluate a translated text by stating what was traded.
Discuss the 'world literature' debate - canons, centres and peripheries, untranseliness, the single world and many public spheres - and take a position with evidence.
Argue from primary texts: build an essay that uses at least three works from three languages, and that names the mediations (translation, edition, adaptation) through which the argument reaches them.

chapters.title: Greece and Rome
chapters.summary: Homer’s epics, Greek tragedy and comedy, and Virgil and Ovid.

chapters.title: The Bible and the Middle Ages
chapters.summary: The Bible as literature, heroic epic and romance, and Dante’s *Divine Comedy*.

chapters.title: Classicism and the Enlightenment
chapters.summary: Molière and Racine, Voltaire and Rousseau, Defoe and Swift, and Goethe’s *Faust*.

chapters.title: Romanticism
chapters.summary: Wordsworth, Byron and Shelley, Hugo, Heine, and Pushkin.

chapters.title: The realist novel
chapters.summary: Stendhal, Balzac and Flaubert, Dickens and the Brontës, and Mark Twain.

chapters.title: Russian literature
chapters.summary: Gogol, Turgenev, Dostoevsky, Tolstoy and Chekhov.

chapters.title: Modernism
chapters.summary: Symbolist poetry, Kafka, Proust, Joyce, Woolf, Eliot and Faulkner.

chapters.title: Post-war and contemporary literature
chapters.summary: Existentialism and the theatre of the absurd, Camus and Beckett, postmodern fiction, and the Nobel laureates of recent decades.

chapters.title: Asian, African and Latin American literature
chapters.summary: *The Tale of Genji* and modern Japanese fiction, Tagore, the *Thousand and One Nights*, Achebe, and Borges, García Márquez and the Latin American boom.

chapters.title: Translation and reception
chapters.summary: How foreign literature reached China, from Lin Shu’s retellings to Lu Xun’s “hard translation” and the present day, and the beginnings of comparative literature.

history.title: Chinese characters set in movable type
history.detail: Chinese type with a small character set demonstrates that print does not require an alphabet: movable type is reinvented independently in two writing systems.
history.people: Hua Sheng; later Korean and Japanese metal type

history.title: The Diamond Sutra printed
history.detail: The earliest dated printed book is a Buddhist text distributed as merit: publication with an audience but no author income.

history.title: Print in Europe
history.detail: Movable type with an alphabet makes fixed editions cheap and errors visible, and creates the conditions for authorship as property.

history.title: Statute of Anne
history.detail: The first copyright statute vests rights in authors for a term: the text becomes a transferable asset.

history.title: A Dictionary of the English Language
history.detail: A single scholar's dictionary stabilises spelling and quotation, making the canonical sentence an instrument of the language.

history.title: Berne convention prelude and international copyright debates
history.detail: The nineteenth century negotiates copyright across borders, and translation becomes a licensed right rather than an act of appropriation.

history.title: First Nobel Prize in Literature
history.detail: The prize creates an annual mechanism for promoting the local to the world, with a jury sitting in one capital.

history.title: The Shape of the Novel in the Eighteenth Century
history.detail: A scholarly history argues that the novel rose with the middle classes - and is later criticised for reading a whole continent through one country.

history.title: UNESCO and the modern translation project
history.detail: Postwar programmes fund translation and index major works, and world literature becomes a policy with a budget.

history.title: The Western Canon
history.detail: A defence of the canon against 'schools of resentment' turns a curriculum argument into a public war about resentment and power.

history.title: What is World Literature
history.detail: A proposal to treat world literature as a mode of reading and of circulation: a work becomes world literature in translation.

references.title: Iliad / Odyssey
references.author: Homer (as transmitted)
references.note: Epic formula, oral composition, and the long editorial life of a text that began as performance.

references.title: Aeneid
references.author: Virgil
references.note: The imperial response to Homer: the second epic that taught Europe how to read the first.

references.title: Mahabharata (selected books)
references.author: attributed to Vyasa
references.note: Encyclopic epic and continuous interpolation: a text that never closed.

references.title: The Tale of Genji
references.author: Murasaki Shikibu
references.note: Court narrative with no precedents in its own language: invention described as a diary.

references.title: Divine Comedy
references.author: Dante Alighieri
references.note: Vernacular theology and the invention of an author's own monument.

references.title: Don Quixote
references.author: Miguel de Cervantes
references.note: The novel reading itself; the founding case for a global genre.

references.title: Faust, Part One
references.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
references.note: World literature as a concept coined by an author reading translations in Weimar.

references.title: Dream of the Red Chamber
references.author: Cao Xueqin
references.note: A manuscript culture's unfinished masterpiece; the case for translation without a fixed source.
